description: Test your knowledge of Posterior triangle of neck.

cards.text: What are the boundaries of the posterior triangle of the neck?
cards.answer: Anterior: posterior border of SCM; Posterior: anterior border of trapezius; Inferior: middle third of clavicle; Apex: meeting of SCM and trapezius at superior nuchal line.

cards.text: Which muscle divides the posterior triangle into occipital and subclavian triangles? What is the clinical significance?
cards.answer: Inferior belly of omohyoid. The occipital triangle (upper, larger) contains CN XI and brachial plexus roots; the subclavian triangle (lower) contains the 3rd part of subclavian artery.

tip.tip: Omohyoid = 'omo' (shoulder) + 'hyoid' — runs from scapula to hyoid, crossing the triangle

cards.text: Where is Erb's point and what emerges there?
cards.answer: Erb's point is at the posterior border of SCM at the midpoint (junction of C5–C6 roots). All cutaneous branches of cervical plexus (great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical, supraclavicular nerves) emerge here.

tip.tip: Erb's point = midpoint of SCM's posterior border; 'Entry point' for cutaneous sensory branches

cards.text: Why is the accessory nerve (CN XI) at risk in posterior triangle procedures? What does it innervate?
cards.answer: CN XI crosses the posterior triangle obliquely from SCM's posterior border to trapezius. Injury during lymph node biopsy causes paralysis of both SCM and trapezius, leading to shoulder droop and neck weakness.

tip.tip: CN XI innervates both SCM AND trapezius — injury = loss of head rotation + shoulder elevation

cards.text: Describe the mechanism and nerve roots affected in Erb's palsy (upper brachial plexus injury).
cards.answer: C5 and C6 roots (±C7) are stretched or torn at Erb's point due to violent separation of neck from shoulder. Results in loss of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion ("waiter's tip" position in severe cases).

tip.tip: Erb's = Upper plexus (C5–C6); cause = violent neck stretch; position = arm hanging by side, hand rotated inward

cards.text: What is the anatomical basis for applying pressure over the 3rd part of the subclavian artery to control upper limb bleeding?
cards.answer: The 3rd part of subclavian artery emerges from behind scalenus anterior and arches over the first rib. Compression against the rib compresses the artery between bone and overlying clavicle, stopping distal bleeding.

tip.tip: Compress 3rd part against 1st RIB (remember: artery 'arches over' rib) — most anterior structure in subclavian triangle

cards.text: What is congenital muscular torticollis and how is it caused?
cards.answer: Fibrosis of SCM (incorrectly called 'sternocleidomastoid tumour of infancy') following birth trauma, commonly from forceps delivery or breech presentation. Causes head tilt toward affected side and chin rotation away.

tip.tip: 'Tumour' is a misnomer — it's actually fibrous scar, not neoplasm; treat early with physiotherapy or surgery if persistent

cards.text: Which nerve roots form the upper, middle, and lower trunks of the brachial plexus?
cards.answer: Upper trunk: C5 + C6; Middle trunk: C7; Lower trunk: C8 + T1. These trunks then divide and form the posterior, lateral, and medial cords.

tip.tip: Remember C5–C6 together (upper), C7 alone (middle), C8–T1 together (lower) — mnemonic: 'Sixes, Sevens, Eights & Ones'
